claims.text: The as-cast high-entropy alloy has a coarse-grained structure.
The as-cast high-entropy alloy has minimal secondary-phase formation.
Severe plastic deformation will produce an ultrafine-grained microstructure with a high grain-boundary density.
Severe plastic deformation will generate a high dislocation density.
Controlled low-temperature aging after deformation will nucleate fine, stable secondary precipitates at grain boundaries.
The increased grain-boundary density will raise strength through grain-boundary strengthening.
The nanoscale precipitates will impede dislocation motion and further increase strength.
Precipitate-induced dislocation pinning will increase Young's modulus.
Coherent secondary phases will deflect cracks.
Coherent secondary phases will distribute strain more uniformly and thereby improve ductility.
Fine precipitates will stabilize grain boundaries against premature fracture and improve fracture resistance.
The processed microstructure will promote beneficial twinning that contributes to improved ductility and fracture resistance.
The processed alloy is expected to exhibit approximately 20% higher yield strength than the as-cast alloy.
The processed alloy is expected to exhibit roughly 15% higher elongation at failure than the as-cast alloy.
The processed alloy is expected to exhibit a measurable increase in Young's modulus relative to the as-cast alloy.
The processed alloy is expected to exhibit greater fracture toughness or fracture-test energy absorption than the as-cast alloy.
Processing under an inert atmosphere will avoid oxidation.
The benefits will be most pronounced in FCC alloys whose phase stability permits dual-phase coexistence.
Predominantly brittle BCC systems or alloys with inherently unstable phases may not obtain the anticipated benefits.
Insufficient aging will fail to form enough precipitates, whereas excessive aging will cause precipitate coarsening and embrittlement.
